subject: Banking
title: Redlining: Banking's Racist Past
description: A quick, practical guide to Redlining: Banking's Racist Past.

hook.text: For decades, US banks drew red lines on maps around Black neighborhoods and refused to make loans there.

buildup.text: The practice began in the 1930s with federal housing maps.

discovery.text: Redlining created a wealth gap that persists today. Black homeownership is 44% versus 74% for white Americans.

twist.text: Redlining was banned in 1968, but studies show banks still deny loans to Black applicants at higher rates.

climax.text: Redlining was legal segregation through banking. The scars of deliberate exclusion are still visible today.

punchline.text: Banned in 1968. Effects still measurable today. Banking's racist scars remain.

quiz.question: What lasting effect has redlining had?
options: A persistent homeownership and wealth gap between Black and white Americans

details.summary: US banks systematically denied mortgages and financial services to Black neighborhoods for decades through redlining, a government-endorsed practice that created racial wealth gaps still measurable today.
details.whyItMatters: Redlining locked generations of Black Americans out of homeownership, the primary wealth-building tool for most families. Its effects persist in property values, credit access, and neighborhood investment.
takeaways: Government maps literally colored minority neighborhoods in red
Banks refused loans in redlined areas regardless of individual creditworthiness
The Fair Housing Act of 1968 banned the practice but effects persist

faq.question: When was redlining officially banned?
faq.answer: The Fair Housing Act of 1968 and the Community Reinvestment Act of 1977 outlawed redlining. However, studies continue to find disparities in mortgage approval rates between white and minority applicants.

faq.question: How much did redlining cost Black families in wealth?
faq.answer: The typical white family has roughly eight times the wealth of a typical Black family. Research attributes a significant portion of this gap to decades of denied homeownership and suppressed property values from redlining.
